chapters.title: Chapter 1: What You Actually Own in a Startup

lessons.title: Equity Shares vs CCPS: Why Indian Startup Investors Usually Get Preference Shares

children.text: Open the allotment filing of almost any venture-funded Indian startup and you will notice something odd. The founders hold equity shares, but the investors who wrote the big cheques mostly hold something called "Series A CCPS" or "Series Seed CCPS". Both groups own the same company. They do not own the same thing. This lesson explains what CCPS are, why professional investors in India insist on them, and what it means for you if you end up holding plain equity while everyone around you holds preference shares.

body.text: CCPS let an investor sit ahead of founders when things go badly and alongside them when things go well. Equity shares only ever sit at the back of the queue.

children.text: What CCPS Actually Are
CCPS stands for
compulsorily convertible preference shares
. Break the name into three parts and it explains itself.

markDefs.definition: Preference shares that must convert into equity shares at a ratio or formula fixed when they are issued, and cannot be redeemed for cash.

children.text: Preference shares.
Under Section 43 of the Companies Act, 2013, a preference share carries a preferential right to dividends and to repayment of capital if the company winds up. It ranks ahead of equity on both.
Convertible.
Each share turns into a set number of equity shares, usually 1 for 1 at the start, with that ratio adjusting for events like bonus issues or a down round.
Compulsorily.
Conversion is not optional. The share cannot be redeemed for cash. It must become equity by a trigger event or a final long-stop date.
That last word is not a technicality. It is the reason CCPS dominate Indian venture deals, and it comes from foreign exchange rules, not company law.

body.label: How FEMA treats preference shares
body.context: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, fully and compulsorily convertible preference shares count as equity instruments. Optionally or partly convertible preference shares are treated as debt and must follow external commercial borrowing rules. A foreign VC that wants to invest as equity has to use CCPS.

children.text: Equity Shares vs CCPS, Side by Side

body.title: What each instrument gives its holder

columns.label: Equity shares (founders, ESOP holders, many small angels)
points: Paid last in a liquidation, after creditors and preference shareholders
Receive dividends only after preference dividends
Rights mostly come from company law and the Articles
No automatic protection if a later round is priced lower

columns.label: CCPS (institutional investors, syndicates, most funds)
points: Rank ahead of equity for return of capital, usually with a negotiated liquidation preference
By law vote only on matters affecting their class, but agreements usually grant voting on an as-if-converted basis
A small fixed preferential dividend, often 0.001% or less
A bundle of negotiated rights attached to the series: anti-dilution, pro-rata, information and veto rights
Conversion ratio can adjust upward in a down round

body.text: That tiny dividend is deliberate. A CCPS might carry a 0.001% non-cumulative dividend, which on ₹2 crore is ₹200 a year. Nobody invests for that. The dividend exists only so the instrument qualifies as a preference share. The real value lies in the liquidation preference and conversion rights.

children.text: Reading a CCPS Term Sheet
When a seed fund invests through CCPS, the key terms of the instrument are usually summarised in a short table like this one.

body.caption: Series Seed CCPS: KrishiLink Technologies Private Limited (illustrative)
headers: What it means for the investor

cells: A separate class with its own rights
Same arithmetic as equity: amount ÷ price
0.001% non-cumulative, plus participation in equity dividends on an as-if-converted basis
Nominal preferential dividend; shares any real dividend like equity
1 CCPS : 1 equity share, subject to adjustment
Starts at 1:1; rises if anti-dilution is triggered
Holder's option at any time; a qualified IPO; or 19 years from issue, whichever is earliest
Conversion is certain; only the timing varies
On exit, takes the higher of its money back or its as-converted share
Votes as though already holding 50,000 equity shares

body.text: A 1:1 conversion ratio today is not a promise of 1:1 forever. Anti-dilution clauses raise the ratio if the company later raises money at a lower price, which hands CCPS holders more equity shares and dilutes equity holders further. Chapter 4 works through the maths.

children.text: Worked Example: Why the Preference Matters

KrishiLink, a fictional Chennai agritech startup, has 2,00,000 founder equity shares. A seed fund invests ₹2 crore for 50,000 Series Seed CCPS with a 1x non-participating liquidation preference. On an as-converted basis the fund owns 50,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 20%.

Two years later the company is sold. Assume it has no debt and the entire sale price goes to shareholders. With a 1x non-participating preference, the fund chooses the better of two options: take its ₹2 crore back first, or convert to equity and take 20% of the sale price.

body.caption: A 1x non-participating preference: the higher of money back or as-converted share, capped at what is available
What the seed fund receives at different sale prices (₹ crore)

body.title: Seed fund's payout: CCPS vs plain equity

children.text: Read the pattern. In modest or disappointing exits, CCPS protect the investor, and every rupee of that protection comes out of the equity holders' share. In a big success the preference is irrelevant, because converting is worth more. The crossover here is a ₹10 crore sale, the point where 20% of the sale price equals the ₹2 crore invested.

body.title: The ₹8 crore sale
body.prompt: KrishiLink is sold for ₹8 crore, with no debt. How much does the seed fund receive, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Converting would give 20% × ₹8 crore = ₹1.6 crore. Taking the 1x preference gives ₹2 crore. The fund takes the higher amount, ₹2 crore, and the founders share the remaining ₹6 crore. Below a ₹10 crore sale, the preference always wins.

body.text: This example is simplified to show how preference works. Real exits involve debt repayment, transaction costs, taxes, ESOP payouts and often several CCPS series with different preferences stacked on top of each other. Lesson 5.2 builds a full exit waterfall.

children.text: The Life of a CCPS

events.title: Allotment
events.description: The company issues CCPS at an agreed price, files Form PAS-3 with the Registrar of Companies and, for a foreign investor, reports the issue under FEMA. The conversion ratio or formula must be fixed at this stage.

events.title: Nominal dividend
events.description: A tiny preferential dividend may be paid if declared. Most loss-making startups declare nothing, and a non-cumulative dividend simply lapses.

events.title: Ratio adjustments
events.description: Bonus issues, share splits and down rounds can change the number of equity shares each CCPS will convert into.

events.title: Conversion or preference
events.description: On a sale, holders compare their liquidation preference with their as-converted payout. Before an IPO, SEBI's ICDR Regulations require outstanding convertible securities to be fully converted into equity before the red herring prospectus is filed.

events.title: Mandatory conversion
events.description: If no trigger has occurred, the CCPS convert automatically on the date fixed in the terms, commonly set just under 20 years from issue.

children.text: This is why the IPO documents of new-age Indian companies routinely describe preference shares being converted into equity shares just before listing. Once the company is public, everyone holds the same equity shares and the special rights attached to each series fall away.

body.title: How conversion is taxed in India

children.text: Indian income tax law does not treat the conversion of preference shares into equity shares as a transfer. In practice this means:
No tax on conversion itself.
You pay nothing when your CCPS become equity shares.
Your cost carries over.
The price you paid for the CCPS becomes the cost of the equity shares you receive.
Your holding period carries over.
The time you held the CCPS counts towards the holding period of the resulting equity shares when you finally sell.

The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026, so section references in older articles on this topic have changed. Confirm the current provisions with a chartered accountant before you plan an exit.
What This Means for You as a Small Investor

If you invest through an angel network or a SEBI-registered angel fund alongside a lead investor, you will usually receive the same CCPS series as the lead. The risk appears when you invest directly and are offered something different.

stats.label: Same price, CCPS
stats.context: You hold the same rights as the lead investor

stats.label: Same price, equity
stats.context: Same cheque, weaker position in every downside exit

stats.label: Lower price, equity
stats.context: A discount can compensate for missing preference

body.title: The equity-only offer
body.scenario: KrishiLink's founders offer you, a Chennai-based chartered accountant, a ₹10 lakh investment in the same round as the seed fund. The price is ₹400 per share, matching the fund, but you will receive 2,500 equity shares, not CCPS. "It's simpler paperwork for a small cheque," the founder explains.
body.prompt: Should you accept as offered? What would you ask for instead?
body.modelAnswer:
Not as offered. At ₹400 you pay exactly what the fund pays, but you get fewer rights. In any sale below ₹10 crore, the fund takes its ₹2 crore preference first and you share what is left with the founders. You carry more risk for the same price.

What to ask for:
1. The same Series Seed CCPS as the fund, on identical terms. The extra paperwork for one more allottee is minimal.
2. If they insist on equity, a lower price that reflects the missing liquidation preference and anti-dilution protection.
3. At minimum, tag-along rights and information rights in the shareholders' agreement, so you are not left behind in a sale or kept in the dark.
4. The full preference stack: every CCPS series, its size and its liquidation preference, so you know exactly how much sits ahead of you.

body.title: Why not optionally convertible?
body.question: A Singapore-based VC fund wants to invest in an Indian startup through optionally convertible preference shares, so it can choose redemption if the company struggles. Why would its Indian lawyers push back?
options: Optionally convertible preference shares are banned under the Companies Act, 2013
Under FEMA they are treated as debt, not equity, and must follow external commercial borrowing rules
Foreign investors can only buy equity shares, never preference shares
Preference shares cannot carry any dividend
body.explanation: Company law allows various kinds of preference shares, but the FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules count only fully and compulsorily convertible preference shares as equity instruments. Anything that might be redeemed for cash is treated as debt under the external commercial borrowing framework, which is rarely workable for a startup investment.

body.title: Name the instrument
body.textWithBlank: For a foreign investor to hold preference shares in an Indian company as an equity instrument under FEMA, the shares must be fully and ___ convertible.
body.explanation: Only fully and compulsorily convertible preference shares count as equity for foreign investment purposes. That single rule is the main reason CCPS became the default instrument in Indian venture rounds.

cards.definition: Compulsorily convertible preference shares: preference shares that must convert into equity shares and cannot be redeemed for cash.
The number of equity shares each CCPS converts into, often 1:1 at issue and adjustable later.
An investor's right to receive a set multiple of its investment before equity holders in a sale or wind-up.
The investor takes either its preference amount or its as-converted share, whichever is higher, but not both.
Treating CCPS as though they have already become equity shares, used for voting and ownership percentages.
The final date by which CCPS convert automatically if no earlier trigger has occurred.
The Companies Act provision limiting preference shareholders' statutory voting to matters directly affecting their rights, subject to exceptions.

points: CCPS are preference shares that must convert into equity. They rank ahead of equity for dividends and return of capital until they do.
FEMA treats only fully and compulsorily convertible preference shares as equity, which is why foreign VCs and most Indian funds use CCPS.
The dividend on CCPS is nominal. The real value lies in the liquidation preference, anti-dilution protection and negotiated rights.
A 1x non-participating preference protects investors in disappointing exits and becomes irrelevant in big ones.
CCPS convert into equity before an IPO, at the holder's option or on a long-stop date.
If you are offered equity at the same price the lead investor pays for CCPS, you are paying more for less. Ask for the same instrument.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. KrishiLink is a fictional company, and the term sheet shown is illustrative. Actual CCPS terms vary widely. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser, a lawyer and a chartered accountant before investing.
